Grounding: AX-5, AX-6, AX-11.
Obligation grounding: AX-5.O2.no_evidence_defaults_blocked, AX-5.O3.authority_cannot_raise_without_derivation, AX-6.O1.closed_world_domain_declared, AX-6.O2.absence_not_negation, AX-6.O3.fact_claims_cite_loci_and_dag, AX-11.O1.grammar_membership_required, AX-11.O2.receipts_and_anti_claims_present, AX-11.O3.prose_alone_is_projection.

A residual is a typed pressure route, not an edge. Before wiring a missing
neighbour, classify the declared domain, source row, target resolution,
fillability, evidence floor, and anti-claim. A candidate route, generated
neighbour hint, basename match, singleton match, or stale projection row is
still pressure; it becomes an edge only when the current source authority row
names the relation and the target resolves under the builder. Bidirectional
substrate representation follows the same floor: principle-to-substrate edges
must be source-derived, and substrate-to-principle evidence may refine governed
ids only when current source rows name the relation. Neither direction is
support proof, projection authority, or permission to launder residual pressure
into an edge. If the substrate cannot name the target from source authority,
keep the gap residual and make the re-entry computable instead of inventing a
relationship or whitening the health card.
nodes.title: Classify residual pressure before wiring

nodes.plain: A doctrine record is not fully active by projection alone. Bind validator receipts, evidence refs, omissions, anti-claims, and authority ceilings on the record before treating its JSON, markdown, routing edge, or public copy as current substrate authority.

analogy.boundary: The medicine-clearance picture only shows that the supporting records must be attached before use; it does not establish that the underlying tests were good, and it does not capture that a readable leaflet, however well written, never raises what the medicine is cleared to do.

maps.analogy: attaching the test results before the medicine is cleared
maps.doctrine: binding validator results to the record before it is authoritative

maps.analogy: the list of what was tested and the known side effects travelling with the medicine
maps.doctrine: evidence refs and stated omissions on the record

maps.analogy: the approved use that limits what the medicine may be dispensed for
maps.doctrine: the authority ceiling bound on the record

analogy.text: A medicine is not cleared for the shelf just because a printed information leaflet for it exists. The test results, the list of what was tested, the known side effects, and the approved use all have to be attached to that medicine before it can be dispensed.

reader.counterexample: A generated doctrine card is cited as the current authority for a rule because the JSON exists and the heading reads confidently, with no validator result records, omissions, or scope limit bound behind it.
reader.does_not_prove: Binding result records to a doctrine record does not make the record correct, witnessed, or complete; it only stops the record from carrying authority its bound checks do not support. The example illustrates the rule and never counts as support for it.

example.text: The release wording gate runs the same claim-language floor over the system's own doctrine copy that it imposes on any other shard, so a record's public line cannot carry authority its bound checks do not support.

reader.governs: The record-and-authority boundary, between a doctrine record existing and being read back as current authority.
reader.plain: A record does not become the trusted version just because a readable copy of it exists. The evidence that its checks passed, the references to its evidence, what it leaves out, and how far it is allowed to claim all have to be attached to the record first.
reader.potential_misread: That a clear, complete-looking record is therefore authoritative. The readable copy is a projection; authority comes only from the checks and limits bound to the record, not from how it reads.
reader.refuses: Reading a record's JSON, markdown, routing edge, or public copy as authoritative on the strength of its existence, before the result records are bound.
reader.requires: Binding the validator result records, evidence refs, omissions, anti-claims, and scope limit on a record before any of its projections is treated as current authority.
reader.why_it_matters: It stops a nicely formatted record from being treated as the trusted source when the checks, evidence, and limits that would back it have not actually been attached.

Grounding: AX-11, AX-12.
Obligation grounding: AX-11.O1.grammar_membership_required, AX-11.O2.receipts_and_anti_claims_present, AX-11.O3.prose_alone_is_projection, AX-12.O1.microcosm_claims_use_same_gate, AX-12.O3.receipt_body_and_doctrine_overclaim_blocked, AX-12.O4.evidence_truth_floor_blocks_release.

receipts, evidence refs, omissions, anti-claims, and authority ceilings on the
record before treating its JSON, markdown, routing edge, or public copy as

nodes.title: Bind receipts before record authority

nodes.plain: Echoing a fixture verdict, registry label, markdown claim, or model answer instead of recomputing it from lower-level evidence.

analogy.boundary: The stale-sign picture shows label-echo; it does not name the deeper rule, which is that the underlying evidence, not the sign, is what a verdict has to be re-derived from.

maps.analogy: yesterday's sign you simply repeat
maps.doctrine: the echoed verdict or label

maps.analogy: the shelf-check nobody actually did
maps.doctrine: the missing recomputation from the evidence

analogy.text: Reading yesterday's 'sold out' sign on a shop and repeating it as today's truth, without checking whether the shelves were restocked overnight.

reader.counterexample: A dashboard shows a component as healthy because its own record said so, with no independent recomputation behind the green.
reader.does_not_prove: Guarding against label echo is a floor under AX-1 and AX-12, not a positive proof that any specific claim is true.

example.text: A monitor replay deliberately feeds a mislabelled trace and confirms the recomputed verdict rejects it, so a wrong label cannot pass by being repeated.

reader.governs: The claim boundary, where a label is mistaken for a derivation.
reader.plain: The mistake of repeating a stored verdict, label, or model answer as if it were true, without re-deriving it from the underlying evidence.
reader.potential_misread: That a label being present means it was checked. The label is just text until something recomputes the verdict beneath it.
reader.refuses: Repeating a fixture verdict, registry label, markdown claim, or model answer as if repetition were proof.
reader.requires: Catching the echo: a recomputed verdict and a negative fixture that fails.
reader.why_it_matters: It is the most common way false confidence spreads: a single unverified label gets quoted as fact all the way downstream.

nodes.plain: Trusting a producer, persona, route, credential, or prior success instead of a checker, proof, policy, or dereferenced capability.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a familiar face is not the same as a confirmed permission. It does not prove the access system itself is correct, that every door in the building is checked this way, or that a confirmed person will behave well once inside.

maps.analogy: letting the person in because the face is familiar and the pass looks right
maps.doctrine: trusting a claim because of its producer or credential

maps.analogy: looking up the access system to confirm clearance for this room today
maps.doctrine: the independent checker or derived authority that should decide it

maps.analogy: the old pass that worked last time
maps.doctrine: a prior green run or standing credential

analogy.text: A building guard waving someone through to a secure room because their face is familiar and they have an old pass, rather than checking the access system to confirm that person is cleared for that room today.

reader.counterexample: A mutation is allowed because the caller holds a long-lived credential and the same route passed last time, with nothing dereferencing current authority or recomputing the claim behind it.
reader.does_not_prove: Refusing producer trust at these witnesses is a floor under AX-2 and AX-3, not positive proof that any granted authority or accepted claim is correct. The example is reader illustration and computes no support; catching identity-based trust in named places does not establish that authority is correctly derived everywhere.

example.text: The tool-authority replay derives whether a call is permitted from the dereferenced capability and policy rather than from the caller's standing identity, so a known caller with no derived authority is refused.

reader.governs: The trust-and-authority boundary, where a producer's identity or a standing credential is mistaken for a check or a derived right.
reader.plain: The mistake of letting something through because of who sent it, what badge it carries, or that it worked last time, instead of independently checking that this request is actually allowed right now.
reader.potential_misread: That a trusted name or a pass that worked before is a safe stand-in for checking. The check has to be made each time against what is actually allowed now.
reader.refuses: Trusting a producer, persona, route, credential, or prior success in place of a checker, proof, policy, or dereferenced capability.
reader.requires: A small checker that decides the certificate, and authority for an effect derived by dereference from tokens, policy, and proof references against current world state.
reader.why_it_matters: Identity is easy to fake or to go stale; a system that trusts the sender rather than re-checking the request looks fine until that sender is wrong or compromised, and by then nothing was actually guarding the door.

nodes.plain: Treating counts, handles, passing validators, or evidence classes as product maturity, release readiness, or whole-system correctness.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a flattering tally can hide an unmeasured part. It does not prove the lines that do report are running well, and it does not establish anything about lines the board never covered.

maps.analogy: the forty-on-time number read as the whole network being fine
maps.doctrine: a count or tally read as the standing of the whole

maps.analogy: a line with no data on the board that could be down
maps.doctrine: a part with no admissible witness that should pin the whole low

maps.analogy: the network is only as good as its worst line, not the on-time count
maps.doctrine: the honest status being the weakest part, not the average

analogy.text: Reading a station board that says forty trains ran on time and concluding the whole network is running well, when several lines simply have no data on the board and could be down.

reader.counterexample: A progress page reports that ninety checks pass and calls the system release-ready, with several required parts carrying no witness at all and the unwitnessed gaps averaged away instead of pinning the whole to blocked.
reader.does_not_prove: Refusing rank-as-score does not raise the standing of any part or make the composite correct. It only keeps the number honest as a projection of the ceiling; the parts beneath it carry exactly the support they were already shown to have, and an uncovered part stays blocked rather than counted.

example.text: The coverage ledger projects how many declared parts are actually materialised and keeps a case that forbids reading an absent entry as covered, so a coverage tally is exposed as a bounded count rather than a completeness claim.

reader.governs: The progress-and-readiness boundary, where a summary number is tempted to stand in for the standing of the whole.
reader.plain: The mistake of reading a single summary number, like how many checks passed, as if it told you the whole thing is finished or ready, when parts you never measured could still be failing.
reader.potential_misread: That more passing checks always means more readiness. Extra passes only help if they cover a part that had no coverage before; repeating the same passing check adds nothing.
reader.refuses: Treating counts, handles, passing validators, or evidence-class names as product maturity, release readiness, or whole-system correctness.
reader.requires: Scoring a composite as the meet of its parts, defaulting an unwitnessed part to blocked, and raising standing only by covering an uncovered obligation, lifting a sub-maximal component, or adding a missing negative case.
reader.why_it_matters: Counting passing checks as a maturity score quietly treats anything unmeasured as if it passed, so a project can look release-ready while a required piece was never even tested.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-3 Rank-as-product-score | AX-5, AX-12 | Treating counts, handles, passing validators, or evidence classes as product maturity, release readiness, or whole-system correctness. |
nodes.title: Rank-as-product-score

nodes.plain: Caching by name, path, route, display label, or producer while basis content has drifted.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a stable label can outlive the thing it points to. It does not prove every card in the catalogue is being checked this way, and one caught mismatch says nothing about whether the rest of the shelves are current.

maps.analogy: the catalogue card filed under the title and shelf location
maps.doctrine: a cached result kept under a stable handle

maps.analogy: the book on the shelf, swapped for a different edition
maps.doctrine: the basis content that has drifted underneath the handle

maps.analogy: checking the actual book on the shelf matches before trusting the card
maps.doctrine: keying reuse on a digest of the content, not the name

analogy.text: Trusting a library catalogue card that says a title sits on shelf B, when the original book was quietly swapped for a different edition and the card was never updated.

reader.counterexample: A view keeps serving a number by its route because the route is unchanged, long after the source it was computed from has been edited underneath it.
reader.does_not_prove: Catching one stale-by-handle reuse at one digest boundary does not prove every cache in the system tracks its basis. This object and its example are reader illustration; they never count as support or proof that freshness holds across the graph, and the source records the freshness component as an open gap rather than a closed one.

example.text: The source-import protocol keys imported material on a content digest and refuses to reuse a copy when the source digest no longer matches, so a drifted source cannot be served by its old path.

reader.governs: The reuse boundary, where a stable handle is mistaken for stable content.
reader.plain: The mistake of reusing a saved answer that is filed under a name or address, after the actual thing behind that name has been changed or replaced.
reader.potential_misread: That an unchanged name means unchanged content. The name can stay identical while what it points to has been replaced underneath.
reader.refuses: Serving a cached result by name, path, route, label, or producer after its basis content has changed.
reader.requires: Keying reuse on a digest of the basis and recomputing or refusing when that digest drifts.
reader.why_it_matters: Pipelines reuse saved results by name to stay fast, but if the underlying source was edited, the name keeps returning yesterday's answer and nobody notices the value is stale.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-4 Cache-across-drift | AX-4, AX-10 | Caching by name, path, route, display label, or producer while basis content has drifted. |
nodes.title: Cache-across-drift

nodes.plain: Treating missing evidence as evidence of absence outside a declared closed domain.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that 'we found nothing' is not the same as 'there is nothing'. It does not establish whether the un-imaged region is actually healthy or not, and it does not turn a properly scanned clear area into a guarantee.

maps.analogy: the region of the body that was never imaged
maps.doctrine: a missing witness, an evidence gap

maps.analogy: reading the un-imaged region as 'all clear'
maps.doctrine: reading that gap as a settled negative

maps.analogy: being able to say 'clear' only for the area actually scanned end to end
maps.doctrine: closing as a negative only inside a declared finite domain where every case is checked

analogy.text: A doctor reading a region of a scan as 'all clear' when that region was never actually imaged, so 'we saw no problem' gets reported as 'there is no problem'.

reader.counterexample: A coverage map shows an area as clear because no failing case was found there, with no declared finite domain behind the closure, so an unsearched region is printed as a settled negative.
reader.does_not_prove: Holding a gap open as unknown does not establish the missing claim either way; it keeps the absence from becoming a false negative, and it grants no support, completeness, or coverage beyond the declared finite domain it names.

example.text: The coverage ledger records what the system has not established as an open gap with a declared scope, and keeps a case that fails if a blank is read as a clean negative, so an unexamined area cannot be reported as proven-absent.

reader.governs: The coverage boundary, where a missing witness is tempted into a settled negative.
reader.plain: The mistake of treating a place where you found nothing as a settled finding that nothing is there, when you may simply not have looked, or not looked everywhere.
reader.potential_misread: That a blank or absence is the same as a confirmed 'nothing here'. Absence of evidence is unknown, not a settled negative, unless the whole area was genuinely covered.
reader.refuses: Treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence outside a declared closed domain.
reader.requires: Holding an uncovered obligation as an open gap, and closing it as a negative only inside a declared finite domain.
reader.why_it_matters: An unexamined gap quietly reads as reassurance, so a coverage map can look finished when it has only stopped looking, hiding risk exactly where no one checked.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-5 Unknown-unknown exhaustiveness | AX-6 | Treating missing evidence as evidence of absence outside a declared closed domain. |
nodes.title: Unknown-unknown exhaustiveness

nodes.plain: Emitting inadmissible numbers or conclusions instead of typed refusal.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a missing input should produce an explicit refusal, not a made-up answer. It does not prove that a dose computed with all the right inputs is correct, and a refusal is not itself a treatment.

maps.analogy: the missing patient weight the dose formula requires
maps.doctrine: a precondition that does not hold

maps.analogy: guessing and handing over a dose regardless
maps.doctrine: emitting a value anyway to keep going

maps.analogy: a written note saying 'dose not computed: weight missing' instead of a number
maps.doctrine: a typed refusal carrying its reason and evidence

analogy.text: A pharmacist guessing and dispensing a dose when the patient's weight, the one input the formula needs, is missing, instead of stopping and saying the dose cannot be worked out yet.

reader.counterexample: A statistics routine returns a coefficient computed past its valid sample size, and a downstream summary reports it as a normal result because it arrived as a number and not as a refusal.
reader.does_not_prove: Refusing one inadmissible emission at a named site does not prove a computation total or its in-domain numbers correct. It keeps the absence of an answer honest; the value it does return is still only as strong as the basis and check beneath it, and this record and its example never count as support for that.

example.text: The finance forecast evaluation component returns a typed refusal when a forecast horizon reaches or exceeds the sample size, or when the statistics dependency it needs is unavailable, rather than reporting a number computed outside its valid range.

reader.governs: The boundary where a partial computation must either answer under its precondition or refuse.
reader.plain: The mistake of producing a number anyway when the thing it needs to be valid is missing, instead of clearly saying 'I cannot answer this and here is why'.
reader.potential_misread: That returning some number is more helpful than refusing. A number produced when its inputs are missing is worse than a refusal, because it hides as a usable result.
reader.refuses: Emitting a meaningless statistic, a silent NaN, or an out-of-domain conclusion just to keep a green path.
reader.requires: Catching the inadmissible value: a totalized result that returns Ok only under a declared precondition and otherwise a refusal carrying a reason and evidence.
reader.why_it_matters: A fabricated number looks just like a real one downstream, so a statistic computed outside its valid range slides into later steps that trust it, while an honest refusal stops the bad value at the door.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-6 Inadmissible number emission | AX-7 | Emitting inadmissible numbers or conclusions instead of typed refusal. |
nodes.title: Inadmissible number emission

nodes.plain: Letting untrusted, private, provider, prompt, credential, or raw-voice material reach a privileged or public sink without provenance and sanitizer transform.

analogy.boundary: This shows the crossing must be gated by what travels with the goods, not by how the truck looks; it does not establish that checking goods at one border post keeps every border in the country clean, and one clean shipment does not mean the whole supply chain is safe.

maps.analogy: the goods arriving at the border
maps.doctrine: the private or untrusted value entering a flow

maps.analogy: entry into the country past customs
maps.doctrine: the public or high-trust place it reaches (the sink)

maps.analogy: the declaration form stating where the goods are from
maps.doctrine: the provenance label that must travel with the value

maps.analogy: the actual inspection that clears the goods
maps.doctrine: the declared cleaning step the value must pass through

maps.analogy: the ordinary truck that makes everyone wave it through
maps.doctrine: the clean-looking final step that hides the breach

analogy.text: Waving a shipment through customs because the final truck looked ordinary, even though no declaration form rode with the goods and no inspection was actually performed.

reader.counterexample: A public page prints a value lifted from a private-adjacent source because the final copy step looked clean, with no provenance carried across the copy and no sanitizing transform between the source and the page.
reader.does_not_prove: Guarding the membrane at named endpoints is a floor under AX-8, not a positive proof of non-interference across the whole graph; endpoint catches are not general propagation, and the example illustrates the boundary rather than computing any support for it.

example.text: The prompt-injection replay carries an information-flow policy with the data, so an untrusted instruction arriving at a tool call is caught at the boundary instead of trusted for having reached a trusted endpoint.

reader.governs: The boundary where material and its trust label cross into a public or privileged sink.
reader.plain: The mistake of letting private or untrusted material reach a public or high-trust place just because the last step looked clean, without a label saying where it came from and without running it through a stated cleaning step first.
reader.potential_misread: That if the last copy step looks tidy and nothing obviously private is visible, the material is safe to publish.
reader.refuses: Untrusted, private, provider, prompt, credential, or raw-voice material reaching a privileged or public sink on a clean-looking final step, with no provenance carried and no declared transform applied.
reader.requires: Carrying a provenance class and ceiling with the value, and routing untrusted material through a declared transform the sink's policy admits before it crosses.
reader.why_it_matters: It is how a system can publish from private-adjacent sources at all without leaking secrets, credentials, or planted instructions onto a public page.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-7 Public/private membrane breach | AX-8 | Letting untrusted, private, provider, prompt, credential, or raw-voice material reach a privileged or public sink without provenance and sanitizer transform. |
nodes.title: Public/private membrane breach

nodes.plain: Performing irreversible mutation without a compensator, rollback receipt, CAS/world-version guard, or explicit irreversible boundary.

analogy.boundary: This shows the obligation to set up a recall path and a balance check before sending; it does not establish that every transaction in the bank is reversible or race-free, only that these specific steps were put in place for this send.

maps.analogy: the money leaving your account
maps.doctrine: the irreversible effect being written

maps.analogy: either a recall option or an upfront note that this transfer cannot be reversed
maps.doctrine: the compensator or declared irreversible boundary

maps.analogy: confirming the balance still matches what you saw before you authorise the send
maps.doctrine: the compare-and-swap check against the expected parent state

maps.analogy: two people moving money from the same account at once
maps.doctrine: two writers racing on the same path

analogy.text: Sending a bank transfer with no way to recall it and without first checking the account balance had not already changed since you looked.

reader.counterexample: A step writes directly over a shared path on the assumption the prior state still holds, with no compare-and-swap and no way to reverse it, so a concurrent write is silently overwritten.
reader.does_not_prove: Guarding the named landing paths against blind writes does not prove every effect in the system is reversible or race-free. It holds the specific obligations AX-9 names, compensator-or-boundary, compare-and-swap, single-writer, over the surfaces that bind them, and the example illustrates that floor rather than counting as support for it.

example.text: The work-landing replay refuses to advance when the expected parent has moved under it and when the head was not advanced as recorded, so a multi-step effect cannot land blindly over a state that has already changed.

reader.governs: The effect boundary, where a mutation is treated as safely landed.
reader.plain: The mistake of making a real, hard-to-undo change while assuming it can always be taken back, when nothing was set up to take it back and nothing checked the situation had not already moved.
reader.potential_misread: That because the normal case completes fine, you can always undo a change later if something goes wrong.
reader.refuses: Writing an irreversible effect with no compensator, no rollback record, no compare-and-swap or world-version guard, and no declared irreversible boundary.
reader.requires: Catching the blind write: a compensator or a declared irreversible boundary, compare-and-swap against the expected parent for multi-step effects, and a single writer per path.
reader.why_it_matters: It stops a change from silently overwriting someone else's concurrent work or landing half-done with no recorded way to undo it.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-8 Blind irreversible mutation | AX-9 | Performing irreversible mutation without a compensator, rollback receipt, CAS/world-version guard, or explicit irreversible boundary. |
nodes.title: Blind irreversible mutation

nodes.plain: Freezing live facts in prose without `as_of`, basis, and rederive contract.

analogy.boundary: This shows that a moving value frozen in permanent text drifts while the text stays put; it does not establish that any value left on the live board is itself currently correct, only that a printed sign loses the ability to be re-checked.

maps.analogy: the train's departure time, which keeps changing
maps.doctrine: the live value (a count or current state)

maps.analogy: printing it onto a permanent sign
maps.doctrine: freezing it into durable prose

maps.analogy: a timestamp saying when this time was accurate
maps.doctrine: the as-of time that should travel with it

maps.analogy: the underlying timetable the departure time came from
maps.doctrine: the basis it was read from

maps.analogy: the live board you could check to get the real current time
maps.doctrine: the rederive route that recomputes it

analogy.text: Printing a train's departure time onto a permanent sign instead of leaving it on the live board, so it keeps showing the old time long after the schedule changes.

reader.counterexample: A page states "the system has 77 components" as a flat fact; the figure was right when typed, but nothing records when it was read or how to recompute it, and it keeps reading as current long after it drifts.
reader.does_not_prove: Blocking unbound live values does not prove a freshness contract is in place everywhere, nor that any carried as-of value is current. It is a floor under AX-10 and P-11; it catches the frozen figure, it does not certify that the figures still bound to a basis are fresh.

example.text: The fact-claim audit treats a volatile count written without a freshness contract as a blocking condition rather than a fact, so a frozen live number is caught instead of trusted because it once was true.

reader.governs: The time-and-freshness boundary, where a moving value is written down as if it were fixed.
reader.plain: The mistake of writing a moving number or a 'current' status into permanent text as if it were a fixed fact, with no note of when it was read, what it was read from, and no way to recompute it.
reader.potential_misread: That because the number was true the moment it was written down, it stays a reliable fact afterward.
reader.refuses: Freezing a count, a "current" state, or a live total into prose with no as-of, basis, or way to re-derive it.
reader.requires: Catching the freeze: a live value must carry an as-of time, a basis, and a rederive route, stay out of durable prose, or be marked a dated snapshot.
reader.why_it_matters: It keeps readers from trusting a stale figure that reads exactly like a live one, long after the real number has moved.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-9 Frozen live fact | AX-10 | Freezing live facts in prose without `as_of`, basis, and rederive contract. |
nodes.title: Frozen live fact

nodes.plain: Granting executable authority to prose doctrine without grammar and receipt obligations.

analogy.boundary: This shows that an unregistered note is only a readable claim, not real access; it does not establish that a pass which is registered is therefore correct or sufficient, only that an unregistered one should not open doors.

maps.analogy: the hand-written note on the door
maps.doctrine: the prose doctrine claiming to govern

maps.analogy: being registered in the building's access system
maps.doctrine: membership in the executable grammar

maps.analogy: stating what proof of access it must show
maps.doctrine: the result-record obligations it must declare

maps.analogy: naming which areas and hours the pass does not cover
maps.doctrine: the stated scope limit (what it does not establish)

analogy.text: Treating a hand-written 'this person may enter' note taped to a door as real access, when it was never entered into the building's access system and never says which areas or hours it covers.

reader.counterexample: A confidently worded policy paragraph is cited as the binding rule for a behaviour, although nothing parses or checks it and it never says what it does not cover.
reader.does_not_prove: Rejecting prose-as-authority is a floor under AX-11, not a positive proof that any admitted standard is correct or complete. It keeps unparsed prose from governing; a standard that does pass the grammar is still only as strong as the obligations it actually carries, and this example illustrates the rule without counting as support for it.

example.text: The executable doctrine grammar accepts a standard as authority only when it parses in the grammar and carries its obligation and scope-limit fields, and keeps a negative case where a prose-only standard that overclaims completeness is rejected rather than admitted.

reader.governs: The boundary between doctrine that governs and prose that only reads as if it does.
reader.plain: The mistake of treating a confidently written paragraph as a binding rule, when the system never accepted it through its formal checks and it never says what evidence it owes or where it does not apply.
reader.potential_misread: That a clearly and authoritatively worded statement is, by virtue of how it reads, a rule the system enforces.
reader.refuses: Granting executable authority to prose doctrine without grammar membership, result-record obligations, and a scope limit.
reader.requires: Refusing authority to any doctrine that is not accepted by the grammar or lacks declared result-record obligations and a stated scope limit, holding it as a projection instead.
reader.why_it_matters: It stops a pile of confident-sounding paragraphs from accumulating as if they were enforced rules nothing can actually check.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-10 Prose-as-executable-authority | AX-11 | Granting executable authority to prose doctrine without grammar and receipt obligations. |
nodes.title: Prose-as-executable-authority

nodes.plain: Exempting Microcosm's own receipts, docs, releases, generated projections, or validators from Microcosm's evidence gates.

analogy.boundary: This shows that the same test must apply to the lab's own samples, removing the self-discount; it does not establish that passing that test makes any sample clean, only that the lab cannot exempt itself from running it.

maps.analogy: the lab's own internal samples
maps.doctrine: the system's own pages, checkers, records, and projections

maps.analogy: the same test run on every outside sample
maps.doctrine: the evidence floor it imposes on external claims

maps.analogy: passing the internal sample on the lab's own word
maps.doctrine: accepting a self-claim without that floor

maps.analogy: the lab's own quality check still having to be tested itself
maps.doctrine: the support evaluator that must meet the floor it computes

analogy.text: A testing lab that strictly retests every sample sent in from outside, but lets its own internal samples through on the lab's say-so without running the same test.

reader.counterexample: A generated page reports the system as verified and complete because its own coverage projection said so, with nothing recomputing that self-claim against the floor the system imposes on external work.
reader.does_not_prove: Refusing the meta exemption does not make the system witnessed, complete, or correct. Admission, support, and this refusal are independent; closing the escape hatch only removes the special pleading, and the worked example illustrates the rule without counting as support for any claim that the system actually meets its own floor everywhere.

example.text: The release wording gate runs the same claim-language floor over the system's own public copy that it imposes on any other source, so overclaiming language in the system's own pages is blocked rather than waved through as a trusted self-statement.

reader.governs: The reflexive boundary, where a claim the system makes about itself is tempted to skip its own gate.
reader.plain: The mistake of letting the system's own pages, checkers, result records, or generated views skip the very evidence test it makes everything else pass, just because it is the system talking about itself.
reader.potential_misread: That a claim is more trustworthy because the system is reporting on itself, so it deserves a lighter check than outside claims.
reader.refuses: A self-assessment of verified, complete, or release-ready that would never pass the floor the system applies to the work it audits.
reader.requires: Routing every self-claim, in a page, validator, result record, or projection, through the same admissibility and refusal floor imposed on external claims.
reader.why_it_matters: It lets the system state its own limits honestly instead of having a flattering self-assessment quietly become a new unchecked claim.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-11 Meta-artifact exemption | AX-12 | Exempting Microcosm's own receipts, docs, releases, generated projections, or validators from Microcosm's evidence gates. |
nodes.title: Meta-artifact exemption

nodes.plain: Using synthetic fixtures as substitutes for available public-safe substrate.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a stand-in must not be passed off as the real input when the real input was available; it does not say practice dummy bags are useless, and it does not establish that the real sample, once used, would give a correct or complete reading.

maps.analogy: the practice dummy blood bag
maps.doctrine: the synthetic fixture standing in for real material

maps.analogy: the real patient sample that was on hand
maps.doctrine: the available public-safe real material

maps.analogy: the result reported as a genuine patient reading
maps.doctrine: the real claim that inherits unearned strength

analogy.text: A lab keeps a bag of practice 'dummy' blood for training, but when a real patient test is needed the technician uses a dummy bag instead of the available real sample and reports the result as a genuine reading.

reader.counterexample: A readiness claim is grounded on a synthetic corpus fixture and reported as real coverage, even though the actual public-safe corpus was available to read.
reader.does_not_prove: Refusing synthetic substitution does not make the real basis correct, complete, or strong, and it does not forbid synthetic fixtures where they are declared as such. It only stops a fabricated input from carrying a real basis's weight; this example is reader illustration and never counts as support for the rule.

example.text: The source-import protocol brings public-safe real material in by manifest and digest so a real claim is grounded on content-addressed real input, rather than a synthetic stand-in fabricated in its place.

reader.governs: The basis boundary, where a claim is grounded on a real or a fabricated input.
reader.plain: The mistake of building a real conclusion on a made-up stand-in input when genuine, shareable material was right there to use, so the fake input quietly lends the conclusion strength it never earned.
reader.potential_misread: That a stand-in is fine because it looks identical to the real thing on the page. The tempting wrong belief is that looking the same means it can carry the same weight.
reader.refuses: Substituting a synthetic fixture for available public-safe real material and letting the claim inherit a strength the real basis never granted.
reader.requires: Grounding a load-bearing claim on available public-safe real material, or holding the claim at bottom and labelling the input synthetic when only a fixture stands in.
reader.why_it_matters: Readers can tell whether a stated result rests on something real and shareable or on a convenient placeholder, so they can judge how much to lean on it.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-12 Synthetic substrate substitution | AX-1, AX-4, AX-8 | Using synthetic fixtures as substitutes for available public-safe substrate. |
nodes.title: Synthetic substrate substitution

nodes.plain: Treating generated receipts as hand-authored source.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a copied card must stay below the book and be redone from it, never used as the origin; it stops there and does not establish that the book itself is correct or up to date.

maps.analogy: the catalogue card copied from the book
maps.doctrine: the generated record derived from a source

maps.analogy: the actual book on the shelf
maps.doctrine: the hand-authored source it should defer to

maps.analogy: writing on the card and citing the card as the book
maps.doctrine: editing or citing the record as origin

analogy.text: Scribbling a correction onto a library's catalogue card and then citing the card as the book, when the card was only ever copied from the book and the book itself still says something different.

reader.counterexample: A generated result record is edited directly and then cited as the origin for a verdict, while the source it was built from is left behind and no longer matches it.
reader.does_not_prove: Keeping generated records bound to their basis does not make either the record or the source correct, and this example illustrates the rule without supporting it. Refusing the inversion only preserves lineage; it does not establish that the basis it points back to is itself true or complete.

example.text: The source-import protocol brings non-secret material in by manifest and content digest, so each imported copy stays bound to the original it was derived from and a basis change forces a recompute rather than letting the copy stand in as source.

reader.governs: The boundary between a generated record and the hand-authored source it derives from.
reader.plain: The mistake of treating an auto-generated summary record as if it were the hand-written original, then editing or quoting that summary as the source while the real source it was built from is left behind and no longer matches.
reader.potential_misread: That whichever copy is already sitting in front of you, with a confident verdict on it, is the thing to edit and cite. The tempting wrong belief is that the handy artifact is the source.
reader.refuses: Treating a generated result record as hand-authored source.
reader.requires: Keeping a generated record bound to its basis by hash and rebuilt from source, so it is recomputed rather than edited or cited as origin.
reader.why_it_matters: It keeps a generated view from quietly outranking the thing it was built from, so a reader knows which artifact is the real origin and which is just a downstream copy.

nodes.statement:
| ID | Violated axioms | Rejected failure shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP-13 Generated-receipt source inversion | AX-4, AX-11 | Treating generated receipts as hand-authored source. |
nodes.title: Generated-receipt source inversion

nodes.plain: Letting public docs imply a hosted service, external service access, source-file mutation, financial or trading decisions, production readiness, affiliation or endorsement, or private-system equivalence that no admissible witness backs.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that a label must not promise a status nothing backs; it does not say the prototype is bad, and removing the inflated label does not settle whether the system could be deployed either way.

maps.analogy: the 'production endpoint' label on the prototype
maps.doctrine: the public page implying an authority

maps.analogy: the uptime, permissions, and partnerships the prototype does not actually have
maps.doctrine: the inflated set of unbacked powers

maps.analogy: relabeling it an honest 'local prototype' until a real deployment exists
maps.doctrine: demoting the claim to its bounded scope when no witness backs it

analogy.text: Labeling a local prototype as a live production endpoint. The label may help a reader see what the prototype resembles, but it cannot grant the uptime, permissions, or partnerships that only the real production system carries.

reader.counterexample: A landing page reads as a ready, hosted product backed by an affiliated provider, when the system is a public reconstruction that hosts nothing, calls no provider, and makes no claim of affiliation.
reader.does_not_prove: Blocking inflated public-authority language does not establish that any specific authority is in fact held; it only refuses the unbacked implication. The example is reader illustration and never counts as support that the system is hosted, deployed, affiliated, or production-ready.

example.text: The release wording gate scans the system's own public copy for release-grade language and blocks a line that would imply hosting, readiness, or whole-system release the system does not hold, so the claim is demoted to its bounded scope rather than published.

reader.governs: The boundary between what a public page implies and what authority the system actually holds.
reader.plain: The mistake of letting a public page's wording imply powers the system does not have, such as being a hosted, ready product, having an outside partner, changing its own source, making financial decisions, or being the same thing as the larger private system, when nothing behind the page backs any of that.
reader.potential_misread: That impressive-sounding wording is harmless because it costs nothing and usually looks right. The tempting wrong belief is that stating a power is the same as holding it.
reader.refuses: Letting public copy imply a hosted service, external service access, source mutation, financial or trading decisions, production readiness, affiliation or endorsement, or private-system equivalence that nothing holds.
reader.requires: Stating only the authority an admissible witness backs, and demoting or refusing the public claim when the witness is absent.
reader.why_it_matters: A reader can trust that what a public page says about itself, like being hosted or ready or affiliated, is limited to what the system can actually back, not free-floating prose.

nodes.plain: Using field vocabulary such as proof, verifier, information flow, world model, or benchmark integrity when the public mechanism only validates a receipt or projection shape.

analogy.boundary: The passport-glance picture shows the name-versus-action gap; it does not list which words are over-strong here, which depends on what the specific mechanism really decides.

maps.analogy: the label 'full background check'
maps.doctrine: the strong borrowed word (verifier, world model)

maps.analogy: the quick glance at the photo
maps.doctrine: the mechanism that only validates a record's shape

analogy.text: Calling a quick glance at a passport photo a 'full background check'. The name promises far more scrutiny than the glance actually performs.

reader.counterexample: A record-shape linter is described as a "world-model verifier", implying it reasons about the world when it only validates a fixture's fields.
reader.does_not_prove: Refusing mechanism theater does not upgrade the mechanism. It keeps the words honest; the underlying check is still only as strong as what it computes.

example.text: The Lean witness compiles a tiny public example through a real verifier and caps its own claim at that bounded scope, rather than calling a schema check a proof.

reader.governs: The boundary between what a mechanism is named and what it actually decides.
reader.plain: The mistake of using strong words like 'verifier' or 'world model' for something that only checks the shape of a record, not the claim those words promise.
reader.potential_misread: That an impressive name reflects an impressive check. The name has to be earned by what the mechanism actually decides.
reader.refuses: Dressing a shape check in proof, verifier, or world-model language.
reader.requires: Naming the real computation and holding the claim to it, with strong words reserved for mechanisms that earn them.
reader.why_it_matters: Strong vocabulary makes a shape check sound far more rigorous than it is, so readers trust it more than it has earned.

nodes.plain: Displaying a declared, inferred, or generated downstream target as an observed runtime effect without evidence of the effect relation.

analogy.boundary: This shows only that arrival must be confirmed at the receiving end before it is displayed as done; confirming one parcel's arrival does not establish that every parcel that went out arrived, and it does not say the address was the right one.

maps.analogy: the 'Delivered' status set the moment the parcel leaves
maps.doctrine: the declared downstream target shown as an observed effect

maps.analogy: no one at the doorstep confirming arrival
maps.doctrine: the missing witness at the receiver

maps.analogy: a truthful 'In transit, not yet confirmed at address' status
maps.doctrine: the honest display: target marked declared and unobserved

analogy.text: Marking a parcel 'Delivered' the instant it leaves the depot, just because the destination address is known, with no one at the doorstep confirming it actually arrived.

reader.counterexample: A status surface shows a memory write as applied at the receiver because the sending step was issued, with nothing observing that the write actually landed there.
reader.does_not_prove: Catching one inflated receiver display is a floor under AX-8 and AX-12, not a positive proof that any effect was achieved. Observing the relation at named receivers does not establish that every declared effect downstream held; the unobserved targets stay marked, not blessed.

example.text: The work-landing replay confirms an agent action actually persisted at its destination before showing it as landed, so a declared target cannot display as a completed effect by intention alone.

reader.governs: The receiver boundary, where an intended or generated downstream target is tempted to display as a witnessed runtime effect.
reader.plain: The mistake of showing an action's intended destination as if the action had already landed there, when nothing has actually checked that it reached the receiving end.
reader.potential_misread: That because the destination is known in advance, showing it as reached is as good as confirming it. The tempting wrong belief is that knowing where something is headed is the same as seeing it arrive.
reader.refuses: Rendering a declared, inferred, or generated downstream target as an observed effect with no evidence that the effect relation held.
reader.requires: Catching the inflation: a witness of the effect relation observed at the receiver, or the target shown as declared and unobserved rather than as an effect.
reader.why_it_matters: A reader can tell apart 'this was sent toward a known target' from 'this was confirmed to have landed', instead of mistaking an intention for a witnessed result.

analogy.boundary: The article-versus-law picture shows a summary cannot outrank its source; it does not capture that the summary must also be recomputed and demoted when the source it describes drifts.

maps.analogy: the news article about the law
maps.doctrine: the generated projection

maps.analogy: the actual text of the law
maps.doctrine: the source contract it summarises

analogy.text: Treating a news article about a law as if it were the law itself, and acting on the article when the two disagree.

reader.counterexample: An edit is made to a generated reference page and treated as canonical, while the contract it was built from is left behind and contradicts it.
reader.does_not_prove: Refusing projection-as-source does not validate the source. It only keeps authority pointed at the executable contract rather than its readable shadow.

example.text: The doctrine projection builder regenerates the readable instances from the routing and markdown sources and checks parity, so the generated copy can never become the authority.

reader.governs: The source-and-projection boundary, where a summary is tempted to outrank its origin.
reader.plain: The mistake of letting a generated page or summary overrule the real contract it was only meant to describe.
reader.potential_misread: That the clearest version is the authoritative one. The source stays authoritative; the summary only points at it.
reader.refuses: Treating a markdown page, generated card, or compact summary as the source it merely describes.
reader.requires: Recomputing the projection from its contract and demoting it when its basis drifts.
reader.why_it_matters: A readable summary is easy to trust, so letting it win over the source quietly replaces the real rule with a description of it.
